description: Navigate the legal boundaries of web scraping and learn techniques to bypass basic anti-bot protections.

slides.title: The Rules of the Road
slides.content:
# Ethics and Legality ⚖️

Before you scrape a website, you must understand the rules.
Web scraping exists in a legal gray area. 

Generally, scraping **publicly available data** is considered legal in many jurisdictions (e.g., the US *hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn* ruling).

However, you can still be sued or blocked for:
1. Violating a site's Terms of Service (especially if you had to log in to see the data).
2. Scraping copyrighted material or Personal Identifiable Information (PII).
3. Crashing a server by sending too many requests (DDoS attack).

slides.title: Robots.txt
slides.content:
# The robots.txt File 🤖

Almost every website has a file located at `https://example.com/robots.txt`.
This file tells search engines and bots which parts of the site they are allowed to scrape.

```text
User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
Disallow: /private/
Allow: /public/

Crawl-delay: 10
```
- `User-agent: *` means these rules apply to ALL bots.
- `Disallow` tells you where NOT to go.
- `Crawl-delay: 10` asks you to wait 10 seconds between requests.

**Always check `robots.txt` before scraping!**

slides.title: Scrapy and Robots.txt
slides.content:
# Enforcing the Rules 🛑

In Python, you can parse `robots.txt` using the built-in `urllib.robotparser`.

But if you use Scrapy, it has built-in support!
In your Scrapy project's `settings.py`, you will find:

```python_not
# Obey robots.txt rules
ROBOTSTXT_OBEY = True
```
If you set this to `True`, Scrapy will automatically read the site's `robots.txt` and refuse to scrape forbidden URLs!

slides.title: Knowledge Check: Ethics
slides.quizQuestion: Where is the first place you should look to see if a website permits automated bots to crawl its pages?
quizOptions: The `robots.txt` file located at the root of the domain.

slides.title: Anti-Bot Protections
slides.content:
# Why am I getting blocked? 🛡️

If a site detects you are a bot, it will return a `403 Forbidden` error, a `429 Too Many Requests` error, or show you a CAPTCHA.

How do they know you are a bot?
1. **Bad Headers:** You didn't send a valid `User-Agent`.
2. **IP Tracking:** You made 500 requests from the same IP address in 1 minute.
3. **Browser Fingerprinting:** Cloudflare or Datadome ran JavaScript to check if your browser actually has a screen, a mouse, and standard fonts installed.
4. **Honeypots:** You clicked a link hidden via CSS (`display: none`) that a real human couldn't see.

slides.title: Fake User-Agents
slides.content:
# Faking your Browser 🎭

The easiest way to bypass basic protections is to rotate your `User-Agent` header.
Instead of hardcoding one, use the `fake_useragent` library!

```bash
pip install fake-useragent
```

```python_not
import requests
from fake_useragent import UserAgent

ua = UserAgent()
# Generate a random user-agent string for Chrome, Safari, etc.
headers = {'User-Agent': ua.random}

response = requests.get('https://example.com', headers=headers)
```

slides.title: Rotating Proxies
slides.content:
# Hiding your IP Address 🕵️‍♂️

If you make too many requests, your IP address will get banned.
To avoid this, you must route your traffic through different IP addresses (Proxies).

```python_not
import requests

# A dictionary of proxies (Usually provided by a paid proxy service)
proxies = {
  'http': 'http://10.10.1.10:3128',
  'https': 'http://10.10.1.10:1080',
}

requests.get('https://example.com', proxies=proxies)
```
In production, you use a **Rotating Proxy API** that automatically assigns a new IP address to every single request.

slides.title: Bypassing Cloudflare
slides.content:
# The Cloudflare Wall ☁️

Cloudflare protects millions of sites. If you try to scrape them with `requests`, you'll get a `403 Forbidden` because Cloudflare runs a complex JavaScript challenge to verify you're a real browser.

Since `requests` cannot execute JavaScript, it fails instantly.

**Solution 1: Playwright/Selenium** (since they run real browsers).
**Solution 2: Cloudscraper**.

slides.title: Using Cloudscraper
slides.content:
# Cloudscraper 🛠️

`cloudscraper` is a Python library that extends `requests` to solve Cloudflare's JavaScript challenges automatically using a Node.js engine under the hood.

```bash
pip install cloudscraper
```

```python_not
import cloudscraper

# Create a scraper instance
scraper = cloudscraper.create_scraper()

# Use it exactly like requests!
response = scraper.get("https://cloudflare-protected-site.com")
print(response.text)
```
*Note: This only works on older/basic Cloudflare protections. For advanced CAPTCHAs, you need specialized services.*

slides.title: Knowledge Check: Anti-Scraping
slides.quizQuestion: Why does a standard `requests.get()` fail when scraping a site protected by Cloudflare?
quizOptions: Because requests cannot execute the JavaScript challenge required to prove it is a real browser.
Because Cloudflare blocks the Python programming language specifically.
Because requests automatically respects the robots.txt file.
Because Cloudflare requires you to send an XML payload.

slides.title: Honeypots
slides.content: # Avoid the Traps 🍯 Some sites set "Honeypots" to catch scrapers. They will put a link in the HTML: `Click here` Since a human can't see it, they will never click it. But a bot that scans the HTML for all `` tags and follows them will click it immediately. Once the bot hits `/trap`, its IP is permanently banned. **Defense:** Check the CSS properties of elements, or only follow specific, targeted links instead of blindly following every `href`.

slides.title: Rate Limiting the Smart Way
slides.content:
# Mimicking Humans 🚶‍♂️

Humans don't click links exactly every 1.000 seconds.
If you use `time.sleep(1)`, server logs will show a perfectly robotic pattern.

You should add **Jitter** (randomness) to your delays!

```python_not
import time
import random

# Wait between 1.5 and 3.5 seconds
delay = random.uniform(1.5, 3.5)
time.sleep(delay)
```

slides.title: Browser Fingerprinting
slides.content:
# You leave a fingerprint 🔍

Advanced anti-bot systems (like Datadome or Akamai) don't just look at IP or User-Agent.
They check:
- Canvas fingerprinting (how your GPU renders graphics).
- Audio fingerprinting.
- WebRTC IP leaks.
- Mouse movement patterns.

Bypassing these requires highly specialized browsers (like Undetected-Chromedriver or Puppeteer-Stealth).

slides.title: CAPTCHA Solvers
slides.content:
# Defeating CAPTCHAs 🧩

When all else fails, a site will throw a reCAPTCHA or hCaptcha at you.

To bypass these automatically, developers use 3rd-party API services (like 2Captcha or Anti-Captcha).
You send the CAPTCHA site key to their API, human workers or AI in the background solve it, and they send you back a token to inject into the page.
*(This is advanced and usually requires a paid API key).* 

**The golden rule of scraping:** The best way to beat a CAPTCHA is to avoid triggering it in the first place (using good proxies and humane delays)!

slides.title: Web Scraping APIs
slides.content:
# The Ultimate Solution 🚀

If you are scraping at scale (millions of pages) and don't want to manage proxies, headless browsers, and CAPTCHA solvers yourself, use a **Scraping API** (e.g., ScraperAPI, Zyte, BrightData).

You send a simple request to their API, and they route it through millions of residential proxies, handle the JavaScript rendering, and solve CAPTCHAs for you.

```python_not
import requests

payload = {'api_key': 'YOUR_API_KEY', 'url': 'https://amazon.com'}
r = requests.get('http://api.scraperapi.com', params=payload)
print(r.text)
```

slides.title: Knowledge Check: Advanced Evasion
slides.quizQuestion: Why should you use `random.uniform(1, 3)` instead of `time.sleep(2)` between requests?
quizOptions: It prevents the requests library from timing out.
It adds jitter, making your bot's behavior look more like a human, preventing detection.
It forces the server to respond faster.

slides.title: Summary
slides.content:
# Summary 🎉

You are now a stealthy (but ethical!) web scraper.

## Key Takeaways
- ✅ **Ethics:** Always respect `robots.txt` and check a site's Terms of Service. Don't scrape PII.
- ✅ **User-Agents:** Use the `fake_useragent` library to disguise your Python script as a real browser.
- ✅ **Proxies:** Route your traffic through different IPs to avoid getting banned.
- ✅ **Cloudflare:** Use `cloudscraper` or Playwright to bypass basic JavaScript challenges.
- ✅ **Honeypots:** Don't blindly follow every invisible link on a page.
- ✅ **Jitter:** Add random delays between requests to mimic human clicking behavior.
- ✅ **Scraping APIs:** For enterprise-level scraping, offload proxy and CAPTCHA management to specialized services like Zyte or ScraperAPI.
